title: Classes: Data and Member Functions
learningObjectives: Define classes with data and member functions.
Understand instance state across separate objects.
Use const member functions for read-only operations.
Separate public behavior from private implementation.

understand.concept: A class groups data and functions. Member functions operate on the object's state; a class can enforce an interface and hide implementation details.
understand.whyItMatters: Classes provide a foundation for object-oriented design and invariants.
understand.explain: Use member functions to keep operations near data; distinguish object state from local variables.

examples.title: Member function
examples.explanation: Member function operates on the object's state.

examples.title: Function with member data
examples.code: class Rectangle{public:int area()const{return width*height;}int width=4,height=3;};\nRectangle r;std::cout<<r.area();
examples.explanation: area reads member values through this object.

examples.title: Separate objects state
examples.code: class Counter{public:void increment(){++value;}int get()const{return value;}private:int value=0;};\nCounter a,b;a.increment();
examples.explanation: Each object maintains its own private value.

examples.title: Const member function
examples.explanation: const member function promises not to modify observable object state.

examples.title: Method call
examples.explanation: Call a member function using dot syntax.

practise.guidedTask: For Classes: Data and Member Functions, trace every example. List each type, object, member, initial value, access path, and state change. Identify where encapsulation or initialization affects correctness.
practise.independentTask: Create a small C++ model focused on Classes: Data and Member Functions (such as a Point, Student, Product, or Account). Include multiple objects, initialization, at least one operation/member access, and test normal, boundary and invalid states. Explain which fields should be public or private and why.
hints: Define the type and its responsibilities before creating objects.
Initialize members deliberately and trace their values.
Use dot for objects and arrow only for pointers.
Keep fields private when they must enforce rules.
Test object creation, valid operations and rejected updates.

questions.explanation: Member functions are part of the class interface.
Dot invokes a member on an object.
Non-static data members belong to each object.
const member functions cannot modify ordinary members.
Member functions can operate on object state.
